entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To join a conversation or discussion by adding your own comment, opinion or information, often briefly.
entries.usage: Very common in meetings, group chats and work emails, as in *Feel free to chime in.* It is friendly and casual, and it often means joining politely while others are talking. Use *chime in with* + the comment and *chime in on* + the topic.
entries.pattern: chime in (with a comment / on a topic)
examples: I was explaining the plan when Sam **chimed in** with a much better idea.
If anyone has used this library before, please **chime in** on the thread.
My grandmother kept **chiming in** with stories from the 1960s all through dinner.

drill.sentence: Everyone in the group chat is suggesting places for the team dinner, so {{chime in}} if you have a favorite.
drill.hint: casually join the conversation with a quick comment (not *weigh in*)

entries.related: *weigh in* — give an opinion, often more seriously or as an expert; *pipe up* — suddenly start speaking, often unexpectedly; *butt in* — interrupt rudely.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To depend mainly on one key factor, so that in the end this factor decides the result.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and explanations, often as *it (all) comes down to …* or *when it comes down to it*. The object is a noun or a *whether* / *how* clause: *It comes down to whether we can afford it.* It sounds plain and natural, not formal.
entries.pattern: it (all) comes down to + noun / whether …
examples: Both job offers are great, so in the end it **comes down to** location.
Whether the model trains in time really **comes down to** how many GPUs we can get.
Honestly, a job interview often **comes down to** the first five minutes.

drill.sentence: The game was tied with ten seconds left, so it all {{came down to}} one free throw.
drill.hint: was decided in the end by (not *hinged on*)

entries.related: *boil down to* — similar, but stresses reducing something to its core; *hinge on* — depend completely on one factor, more formal; *depend on* — plain and general.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To have something as its basic or most important point, once you remove the details.
entries.usage: Used in conversation, talks and explanations to simplify a complex issue: *It all boils down to trust.* The transitive form *boil something down (to …)* means to shorten or summarize it. Very close to *come down to*, but it stresses reducing a complex thing to its core.
entries.pattern: X (all) boils down to Y; boil something down to its essentials
examples: Once you strip away the jargon, the new policy **boils down to** a pay cut.
Most of these debugging stories **boil down to** a wrong assumption about the data.
For a lot of couples, the fights **boil down to** money and chores.

drill.sentence: The coach's whole philosophy can be {{boiled down to}} three words: defense wins championships.
drill.hint: summarized, once the details are stripped away (a cooking image)

entries.related: *come down to* — very similar, stresses the deciding factor; *sum up* — summarize; *in a nutshell* — in very few words.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To solve the last small problems or disagreements in something, often about details, so that it works smoothly.
entries.usage: Common at work and in negotiations: *iron out the details, the kinks, our differences*. It suggests the main plan or deal is fine and only small problems remain. A noun object usually follows *out*, but a pronoun goes in the middle: *iron it out*.
entries.pattern: iron out the details / kinks / differences
examples: The deal is mostly done; the lawyers just need to **iron out** a few details.
We're still **ironing out** the kinks in the new scheduler, so expect a few failed jobs this week.
My roommate and I sat down and **ironed out** who pays for what.

drill.sentence: The two sides agree on the big picture but still need to {{iron out}} their differences on pricing.
drill.hint: smooth away, like wrinkles in a shirt (not *work out*)

entries.related: *work out* — more general, solve or plan; *hash out* — discuss in detail until you agree; *smooth over* — make a conflict seem smaller, often without solving it.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To explain something very clearly and in full detail, so that nobody can misunderstand it.
entries.usage: In neutral use, rules, contracts and guidelines *spell out* conditions or steps. With a person as subject, it often means saying something obvious very directly; *Do I have to spell it out for you?* is impatient and a little rude. A pronoun goes in the middle: *spell it out*.
entries.pattern: spell out + details / terms; spell it out (for someone)
examples: The new guidelines **spell out** exactly what counts as a conflict of interest.
He kept dropping hints, but she didn't get it until he **spelled it out**.
In the README, **spell out** every step needed to reproduce the results.

drill.sentence: I know you're upset, but I can't fix it unless you {{spell out}} exactly what I did wrong.
drill.hint: explain clearly and in full

entries.related: *lay out* — present a plan or argument in an organized way; *make explicit* — more formal; *drop a hint* — the opposite, suggest without saying it.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To add details and substance to an idea, plan or draft that so far exists only in outline.
entries.usage: Common at work, in writing and in teaching: *flesh out the proposal, the plan, the characters*. It suggests the basic structure is there but still thin. A noun object usually follows *out* (*Could you flesh out the budget section?*), and a pronoun goes in the middle: *flesh it out*.
entries.pattern: flesh out + idea / plan / draft / section
examples: The idea is promising, but you'll need to **flesh it out** before we pitch it to investors.
My editor asked me to **flesh out** the second chapter with more examples.
In the second season, the writers finally **flesh out** the minor characters.

drill.sentence: Right now the plan is just a few bullet points, so let's {{flesh it out}} before Friday's meeting.
drill.hint: add detail and substance, like putting meat on bare bones

entries.related: *expand on* — say more about a point; *elaborate on* — more formal; *pad* — add unnecessary material just to make something longer.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To develop in a successful way or turn out as hoped.
entries.usage: Informal and very common in speech, mostly in the negative or in questions: *It didn't pan out*, *Let's see if it pans out.* It is used for plans, job offers, leads, deals and research ideas. It is intransitive: the plan, lead or idea is the subject, never the person.
entries.pattern: didn't pan out; see if / how it pans out
examples: I had a job offer in Denver, but it didn't **pan out**, so I'm still looking.
We tried pruning the model, but the speedup never really **panned out**.
If the new restaurant **pans out**, the owners plan to open a second location.

drill.sentence: My cousin quit his job to sell hot sauce online, and so far it's {{panning out}} better than anyone expected.
drill.hint: going well (informal; not *working out* or *turning out*)

entries.related: *work out* — same meaning, more common and neutral; *turn out* — develop in a certain way, good or bad; *fall through* — fail to happen, about plans and deals.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To happen or develop in a particular way over time, especially when the result is not yet clear.
entries.usage: Common in news, analysis and conversation about events, conflicts and plans, often with *how*: *We'll see how it plays out.* In this sense it is intransitive, so the event is the subject. A scene or story can also *play out* somewhere: *The feud played out on social media.*
entries.pattern: see / watch how it plays out
examples: It's too early to say how the trade dispute will **play out**.
Let's run the new setup for a week and see how it **plays out** before changing anything.
The family feud **played out** on Facebook, where all their friends could see it.

drill.sentence: My two best friends just started dating, so I'm going to sit back and watch it all {{play out}}.
drill.hint: develop, step by step, over time (not *unfold*)

entries.related: *unfold* — similar, a bit more formal; *turn out* — focuses on the final result; *pan out* — succeed as hoped.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: Of news or a fact: to become fully understood or felt, usually some time after you first hear it.
entries.usage: Very common for big news, good or bad: *It hasn't sunk in yet.* The subject is the news or fact, not the person, and it often comes with *yet*, *finally* or *start to*. *Let that sink in* is a popular, slightly dramatic way to ask listeners to think about a fact.
examples: I got the job last week, but it still hasn't **sunk in**.
It took a few minutes for the news of the layoffs to **sink in**.
We spend more on cloud computing than on salaries. Let that **sink in**.

drill.sentence: When the doctor said the tumor was benign, it took a moment for her words to {{sink in}}.
drill.hint: be fully understood and felt (not *register*)

mistake.wrong: I still haven't sunk in that I got the job.
mistake.right: It still hasn't sunk in that I got the job.
mistake.why: The news or fact *sinks in*; the person who understands it is not the subject.

entries.related: *dawn on someone* — a fact becomes clear to you for the first time; *register* — be noticed or understood, often in the negative; *hit someone* — a sudden emotional realization.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: Of something unpleasant, such as bad weather, an illness or a feeling: to begin and seem likely to continue for some time.
entries.usage: Typical subjects are *winter, rain, panic, fatigue, boredom, infection* and *reality*. It is intransitive, so the unpleasant thing *sets in* by itself. It often follows *once*, *before* or *begin to*: *before panic sets in*.
entries.pattern: winter / panic / fatigue + sets in
examples: By noon the rain had **set in**, so we moved the birthday party into the garage.
By hour ten of the hackathon, fatigue had **set in**, and the bugs started piling up.
Clean the wound right away, or an infection could **set in**.

drill.sentence: The first week of the diet was fine, but by the third week boredom had {{set in}}.
drill.hint: begun and looked likely to last (not *crept in*)

entries.related: *kick in* — start to take effect, often of something useful (*the painkillers kicked in*); *creep in* — appear slowly and quietly; *take hold* — become established and hard to stop.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To notice something subtle or not openly stated, such as a mood, a hint, a tone or a small detail.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and at work: *pick up on a hint, someone's mood, a tone, social cues*. It suggests sensitivity to small signals and often follows *quick to* or *never*. It is inseparable: the thing noticed always comes after *on*, even when it is a pronoun (*picked up on it*).
entries.pattern: pick up on + hint / mood / tone / cues
examples: Kids are quick to **pick up on** tension between their parents, even when nobody says anything.
She dropped a few hints about her birthday, but her boyfriend never **picked up on** them.
A good interviewer **picks up on** small hesitations and asks a follow-up question.

drill.sentence: My dog always {{picks up on}} my mood; when I'm sad, he comes and rests his head on my lap.
drill.hint: notices without being told (not *senses*)

entries.related: *notice* — plainer, for anything you see; *catch on* — finally understand something; *pick on someone* — a different verb: bully or tease them unfairly.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To find a meaning, intention or importance in something that is probably not really there.
entries.usage: Very often with *too much*: *Don't read too much into it*. Common in conversation about texts, comments and body language, and in news about polls or one-off results. The amount goes between *read* and *into* (*read too much / a lot / nothing into*), and the thing you interpret always comes after *into*.
entries.pattern: read (too much / a lot / nothing) into + something
examples: He didn't reply to my text for two hours, but I'm trying not to **read too much into** it.
Analysts warn against **reading too much into** a single month of job numbers.
She's polite to everyone, so don't **read anything into** the fact that she smiled at you.

drill.sentence: It was just one bad game, so don't {{read too much into}} the loss; the team is still in first place.
drill.hint: see more significance in (not *make too … of*)

entries.related: *overinterpret* — the formal one-word equivalent; *make too much of* — treat as more important than it is; *take something at face value* — the opposite, accept it as it seems.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To change your opinion, slowly or after resisting, and finally accept an idea or agree with someone.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, politics and news: *She'll come around*, *come around to the idea that …*. It suggests a gradual change after doubts or opposition. It is intransitive, so the idea follows *to* and never goes between *come* and *around*; British English also says *come round*.
entries.pattern: come around (to the idea / view that …)
examples: My dad hated the idea of me moving to New York, but he eventually **came around**.
More and more cities are **coming around to** the idea of car-free downtown streets.
The coach had doubts about the young goalie, but he's **come around**, and she starts every game now.

drill.sentence: Mom refused to get a dog for years, but she finally {{came around}} when she saw how responsible we were.
drill.hint: changed her opinion and agreed (not *gave in*)

entries.related: *come round* — the British form; *give in* — stop resisting, often unwillingly; *win someone over* — persuade someone to support you.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To believe or accept an idea, claim or plan, often too readily or without questioning it.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, business and opinion writing: *buy into the hype, the idea, the myth*. In the negative it means you are not convinced (*I don't buy into that*); at work it can also mean real support for a plan, as in the noun *buy-in*. The idea always comes after *into*.
entries.pattern: buy into the hype / the idea / the myth (that …)
examples: I never **bought into** the hype about that diet; it's just eating less under a fancy name.
If the nurses don't **buy into** the new shift system, it won't work.
Too many people **buy into** the myth that you need a college degree to succeed.

drill.sentence: My uncle has never {{bought into}} the idea that you need an expensive gym to get in shape; he works out in his garage.
drill.hint: believed or accepted (not *fallen for*)

entries.related: *fall for* — be tricked into believing; *buy it* — informal, believe a claim; *get buy-in* — work jargon, get people to support a plan.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To delay doing or deciding something for now, usually until you know more or the timing is better.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, at work and in news: *hold off on buying a house*, *hold off until next week*. With *on* it takes a noun or *-ing*; it can also take *-ing* directly, as in *hold off making a decision*. In this sense nothing goes between *hold* and *off*.
entries.pattern: hold off (on + noun / -ing) (until …)
examples: Let's **hold off on** booking the flights until we know the exact dates.
Many buyers are **holding off** until mortgage rates come down.
The doctor said I could **hold off on** surgery for now and try physical therapy first.

drill.sentence: If you're not sure about the color, {{hold off on}} painting the whole living room and test a small patch first.
drill.hint: delay for now (not *put off*)

entries.related: *put off* — postpone, often to a later date and sometimes out of laziness; *wait on* — informal, mainly US, wait before doing; *hold back* — not do or say something, often from caution.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To tell someone the details or news that they missed or do not know yet.
entries.usage: Very common at work and among friends: *Can you fill me in?*, *I'll fill you in later*. The person almost always goes between *fill* and *in*, and *on* introduces the topic: *fill her in on the plan*. Without a person, *fill in* has other meanings, such as *fill in for someone* (replace them at work).
entries.pattern: fill someone in (on + topic)
examples: I missed the first half of the meeting. Can someone **fill me in**?
Call me tonight and **fill me in on** the wedding; I want every detail.
Before the trip, our guide **filled us in on** a few local customs.

drill.sentence: I was out of town last week, so could you {{fill me in}} on what happened at the neighborhood meeting?
drill.hint: tell me the details I missed (not *catch me up*)

mistake.wrong: Can you fill in me on the details?
mistake.right: Can you fill me in on the details?
mistake.why: With separable phrasal verbs, a pronoun object must go between the verb and the particle.

entries.related: *catch someone up* — very similar, common in the US; *bring someone up to speed* — give them all the latest information, often at work; *brief someone* — more formal, give official information.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To settle or agree on something definitely, such as a date, a price or a detail, so it is no longer uncertain.
entries.usage: Common at work and in planning: *nail down a date, the details, a deal, the budget*. It suggests moving from vague talk to a firm decision. A noun object can go before or after *down* (*nail down the date*, *nail the date down*), but a pronoun must go in the middle: *nail it down*.
entries.pattern: nail down + a date / the details / a deal
examples: We still need to **nail down** a date for the wedding before we can book the venue.
Let's **nail down** the budget this week so the design team can get started.
The two teams are close to a trade, but they haven't **nailed down** the final details.

drill.sentence: We've talked about a family trip for months; now we just need to {{nail down}} where we're actually going.
drill.hint: settle once and for all, as if with a hammer

entries.related: *pin down* — establish exactly, often a fact or a cause; *firm up* — make plans more definite; *finalize* — more formal, complete the last details.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To establish something exactly, such as a cause, a time, a number or a definition.
entries.usage: Often used about things that are hard to identify precisely, so it appears with *hard to*, *try to* or *can't quite*: *I can't quite pin it down*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*pin it down*); a noun can go before or after *down*. With a person as object, *pin someone down* means making them give a clear answer or commitment.
entries.pattern: pin down + the cause / the date / exactly what …
examples: Something about the house felt strange, but I couldn't quite **pin it down**.
Historians have struggled to **pin down** the exact date of the painting.
Once we **pinned down** which food was giving our son hives, life got a lot easier.

drill.sentence: The wine has a flavor I know but can't {{pin down}}; is it cherry or plum?
drill.hint: identify exactly (not *place* or *put my finger on*)

entries.related: *pinpoint* — locate or identify exactly, a bit more formal; *nail down* — settle something definitely, like a date; *put your finger on* — identify exactly, usually in the negative.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To complete something you started, promised or threatened to do, instead of stopping halfway.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, management and parenting advice: *follow through on a promise, a threat, a plan*; *follow through with* is also used. It is about reliability, as in *He never follows through*, and the noun is *follow-through*. In this pattern the task comes after *on* or *with*, not between *follow* and *through*.
entries.pattern: follow through on / with + promise / threat / plan
examples: He promised to fix the fence, but he never **followed through**.
If you threaten to take away your kid's phone, you have to **follow through on** it.
Customers will forgive a late delivery, but not a company that never **follows through on** its promises.

drill.sentence: I signed up for the gym in January, but I didn't {{follow through}}; I've only gone twice.
drill.hint: keep going with what I'd started (not *stick with it*)

entries.related: *see something through* — continue until something difficult is finished; *keep your word* — do what you promised; *flake* — informal, fail to do what you said you would.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To take on more responsibility or make a bigger effort when a situation needs it, often when someone else cannot.
entries.usage: Common in sports, work, families and news, often as praise or a call to action: *Someone needs to step up*. In this sense it is intransitive, and *step up to* + a challenge is also common (*step up to the plate*). *Step something up* (separable) is a different sense, "increase it": *step up security*.
entries.pattern: step up (and + verb); step up to + a challenge
examples: When our manager got sick, Priya **stepped up** and ran the whole project.
After their mom's surgery, the older kids really **stepped up** around the house.
With the star injured, the backup quarterback **stepped up** and threw three touchdowns.

drill.sentence: With half the volunteers out sick, the teenagers {{stepped up}} and served dinner to two hundred people at the shelter.
drill.hint: took on extra responsibility when it was needed (the particle isn't *in*)

entries.related: *step in* — get involved to help or to stop something; *rise to the occasion* — do well in a difficult situation; *pull your weight* — do your fair share.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To join others in helping with a shared task, or in giving money for something.
entries.usage: Very common in American conversation about chores, events, gifts and community work: *Everyone pitched in*. It sounds friendly and cooperative. Use *pitch in with* + a task or *pitch in for* + a gift, and put an amount right after *in*: *We each pitched in twenty dollars*.
entries.pattern: pitch in (with + task / for + gift)
examples: When the storm knocked down our fence, the whole block **pitched in** to help rebuild it.
My coworkers all **pitched in** to buy a fancy espresso machine for the break room.
If everyone **pitches in** with the dishes, we'll be done in ten minutes.

drill.sentence: The house was a mess after the party, but everybody {{pitched in}}, and it was clean by midnight.
drill.hint: joined in to help with the work (not *helped out* or *chipped in*)

entries.related: *chip in* — give money or help, very similar; *help out* — neutral; *muck in* — British, share hard or dirty work.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To confuse or distract someone so that they lose their focus, rhythm or sense of what is happening.
entries.usage: Very common in American conversation; the subject is usually an unexpected event, question or change: *That question really threw me off*. The person normally goes between *throw* and *off*, and a pronoun must (*it threw me off*). *Throw someone off their game* means make them perform worse than usual.
entries.pattern: something throws someone off (their game / rhythm)
examples: The interviewer's first question was so unexpected that it completely **threw me off**.
Losing an hour of sleep in March always **throws me off** for a few days.
The crowd noise **threw the young pitcher off**, and he walked three batters in a row.

drill.sentence: I was doing fine at my piano recital until someone's phone rang, and that {{threw me off}}.
drill.hint: broke my concentration and confused me (not *distracted me*)

entries.related: *put someone off* — make someone lose interest, or in British English distract them; *rattle* — make someone nervous; *throw someone* — informal, confuse them (*His answer threw me*).

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To annoy, upset or affect someone emotionally, often slowly over time.
entries.usage: Common in conversation: *It's starting to get to me*, *Don't let it get to you*. The subject is usually a situation, a noise, criticism or pressure, and the person always comes after *to*. It can also mean being deeply moved, as in *That movie really got to me*.
entries.pattern: something gets to someone; don't let it get to you
examples: The constant noise from the construction next door is really starting to **get to me**.
Don't let the comments online **get to you**; those people don't even know you.
I don't usually cry at movies, but the ending really **got to me**.

drill.sentence: She acts tough, but all the criticism in the press is clearly {{getting to her}}.
drill.hint: affecting her emotionally (phrasal verb with *to*; not *bothering* or *wearing on*)

entries.related: *get on someone's nerves* — annoy, about small repeated things; *get under someone's skin* — annoy deeply; *wear someone down* — exhaust them slowly.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To start an event, a meeting, a season or a process, often in a lively way.
entries.usage: Very common at work and in event talk: *kick off the meeting*, *kick off the season*; it also works without an object, as in *The festival kicks off on Friday*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*kick it off*); a noun can go before or after *off*. The noun *kickoff* is the start of a football game or of a project.
entries.pattern: kick off + meeting / season / campaign (with + something)
examples: Let's **kick off** the meeting with a quick update from each team.
The city **kicks off** its summer concert series next weekend in the park.
To **kick things off**, the host asked everyone to share their most embarrassing moment.

drill.sentence: An Olympic champion will {{kick off}} the marathon by firing the starting gun at seven.
drill.hint: officially start (informal, not *start off*)

entries.related: *get the ball rolling* — informal, start an activity; *launch* — start something big, like a product or a campaign; *wrap up* — the opposite, finish.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To start to take effect or to start working, often after a delay.
entries.usage: Used for medicine, caffeine, adrenaline, insurance coverage, new laws and heating: *The painkillers kicked in*. It is intransitive, so the drug or system is the subject. In informal American English, *kick in* + an amount can also mean "contribute money," which is a different sense.
entries.pattern: the medicine / caffeine / heat + kicks in
examples: I took two ibuprofen, and after twenty minutes they finally **kicked in**.
The new minimum wage **kicks in** on January first.
In the last mile of the race, my adrenaline **kicked in**, and I sprinted to the finish.

drill.sentence: I'm useless in the morning until the caffeine {{kicks in}}.
drill.hint: starts to take effect (not *hits*)

entries.related: *take effect* — more formal; *set in* — something unpleasant begins and lasts; *wear off* — the opposite, stop having an effect.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To launch or introduce a new product, service or policy, often in stages or across many places.
entries.usage: Very common in business, tech and government news: *roll out a feature, an update, a program nationwide*. It suggests a planned launch to many people, often step by step. A pronoun goes in the middle (*roll it out*), and the noun is *rollout*.
entries.pattern: roll out + product / policy / service (to + users / nationwide)
examples: The coffee chain is **rolling out** its new menu in all stores next month.
The school district is **rolling out** laptops to every student, starting with the high schools.
My bank just **rolled out** a feature that lets you split bills with friends.

drill.sentence: The city plans to {{roll out}} the new bike-share program one neighborhood at a time.
drill.hint: introduce gradually, area by area (not *phase in*)

entries.related: *launch* — start or introduce, without the idea of stages; *phase in* — introduce gradually, often rules or taxes; *pull* — withdraw a product.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To increase the amount, speed or intensity of something, often steadily or quickly.
entries.usage: Common in business, news and sports: *ramp up production, hiring, efforts, pressure*. It also works without an object, as in *Production is ramping up*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*ramp it up*), and the opposite is *ramp down*.
entries.pattern: ramp up + production / efforts / pressure / spending
examples: The factory is **ramping up** production to meet holiday demand.
With the race a month away, I'm **ramping up** my training to forty miles a week.
Police have **ramped up** patrols in the neighborhood after a string of break-ins.

drill.sentence: The airline is {{ramping up}} the number of flights to Florida for the winter season.
drill.hint: steadily increasing (not *stepping up*)

entries.related: *step up* — increase effort or activity, very similar; *scale up* — make bigger in size or scope; *wind down* — the opposite, gradually reduce.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To find a way to avoid or get past a problem or limit without actually solving or removing it.
entries.usage: Common at work, in tech and in everyday planning: *work around a bug, a schedule, a rule, someone's allergies*. The problem always comes after *around*, even a pronoun: *work around it*. The noun *workaround* means a temporary fix.
entries.pattern: work around + problem / schedule / limitation
examples: The elevator was broken, so the movers had to **work around** it and carry everything up the stairs.
Planning dinner for my family means **working around** one vegan, two picky kids and a peanut allergy.
Until the bug is fixed, you can **work around** it by restarting the app.

drill.sentence: Our wedding venue doesn't allow live music after nine, so we'll have to {{work around}} that rule.
drill.hint: plan within the limit it sets, not find a loophole

entries.related: *get around* — avoid a rule or problem, often with a clever trick or loophole; *deal with* — handle a problem directly; *workaround* — the noun, a temporary fix.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To include something as one of the things you consider when you calculate, plan or decide.
entries.usage: Common in planning, budgeting and advice: *factor in travel time, taxes, delays, the cost of …*. A noun usually goes after *in* (*factor in the tip*), and a pronoun goes in the middle (*factor it in*). *Factor into* is different: *Cost factored into my decision* means it played a role.
entries.pattern: factor in + time / costs / delays
examples: Coaches have to **factor in** the weather when they choose a game plan.
The drive takes three hours, but you should **factor in** traffic around Philadelphia.
Once you **factor in** the tip and tax, dinner cost almost a hundred dollars.

drill.sentence: The house looks cheap, but you need to {{factor in}} the cost of a new roof and furnace.
drill.hint: include in your calculation (not *account for*)

entries.related: *take into account* — consider, slightly more formal; *allow for* — plan for something possible, like delays; *leave out* — the opposite, not include.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To make time, money, space or people available for another use, usually by removing or finishing something else.
entries.usage: Common at work and at home: *free up time, space, money, your afternoon*. It also works with people, as in *That frees me up to cook*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*free it up*); a noun can go before or after *up*.
entries.pattern: free up + time / space / money; free someone up to + verb
examples: Canceling three streaming services **freed up** almost forty dollars a month.
Moving the meeting to Thursday **frees up** my whole Wednesday afternoon.
Having my parents take the kids for the weekend **freed us up** to repaint the bedroom.

drill.sentence: Donating the boxes of old toys will {{free up}} plenty of room in the garage.
drill.hint: make available (phrasal verb; not *open up* or *clear out*)

entries.related: *clear out* — empty a space by removing things; *make room for* — create space for something; *tie up* — the opposite, keep money or people busy.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To accept an offer or invitation that someone has made to you.
entries.usage: Common in friendly conversation and emails: *I might take you up on that*, *I'll take you up on your offer*. The person always goes between *take* and *up*, and the offer follows *on*. It is used for offers and invitations, not for orders or requests.
entries.pattern: take someone up on their offer / invitation
examples: You said I could stay with you in Seattle; I might **take you up on** that this summer.
Several employees **took the company up on** its offer of early retirement.
When my neighbor offered to watch the dog, I **took her up on** it right away.

drill.sentence: Is your offer to help us move still good? We'd love to {{take you up on}} it.
drill.hint: accept what you offered (the pronoun goes in the middle)

mistake.wrong: I'd love to take up on your offer.
mistake.right: I'd love to take you up on your offer.
mistake.why: The person must go between *take* and *up*; without a person, say *take up the offer* or *accept the offer*.

entries.related: *take up an offer* — accept it, without naming the person; *jump at* — accept eagerly; *turn down* — the opposite, refuse.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To become even more committed to a risky position, claim or plan, especially after it has been criticized or has gone badly.
entries.usage: Very common in American news, politics and business: *double down on a claim, a strategy, a bet*. It often sounds critical and suggests stubbornness, but it can also praise a bold strategy. The thing follows *on*; nothing goes between *double* and *down*.
entries.pattern: double down on + claim / strategy / bet
examples: Instead of apologizing, the restaurant owner **doubled down** and posted an even ruder reply to the review.
After a weak year, the carmaker is **doubling down on** electric trucks.
My brother lost fifty bucks on the first game and then **doubled down** on the second one.

drill.sentence: When people laughed at her idea for a dog bakery, she {{doubled down}} and opened a second location.
drill.hint: committed even more strongly (not *went all in*)

entries.related: *dig in your heels* — refuse to change your position; *go all in* — risk everything; *back down* — the opposite, give up a position.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To appear or happen unexpectedly, usually a problem, an issue or a new thing.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and at work for problems, questions and new places that appear without warning: *A few issues cropped up*. It is intransitive, so the problem is the subject, and it often follows *keep*. For personal excuses, Americans more often say *Something came up*.
entries.pattern: a problem / an issue + crops up; keep cropping up
examples: If any problems **crop up** while we're away, call our neighbor.
New coffee shops keep **cropping up** all over the neighborhood.
The same complaint **crops up** again and again in the customer reviews.

drill.sentence: We planned a quiet weekend, but problems kept {{cropping up}}: first the car, then the water heater.
drill.hint: appearing unexpectedly (not *coming up* or *popping up*)

entries.related: *come up* — arise, very similar and more neutral; *pop up* — appear suddenly, informal; *spring up* — appear quickly in large numbers, like new buildings.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be slowed down or stuck because of too many details, problems or tasks, so that you make little progress.
entries.usage: Common at work and in advice, often as a warning: *Let's not get bogged down in the details*. It is used with *get* or *be* plus *in* + the obstacle (*details, paperwork, red tape*). The active *bog someone down* exists, but this passive-like form is far more common.
entries.pattern: get / be bogged down in + details / paperwork
examples: Let's not **get bogged down** in the details; we just need a rough plan for now.
The bill **got bogged down** in committee and never came to a vote.
I wanted to read more this year, but I **got bogged down** in a nine-hundred-page novel.

drill.sentence: We bought the fixer-upper in May, but we {{got bogged down}} in permits and didn't start work until October.
drill.hint: were held back and stuck, as if in mud (not *got stuck*)

entries.related: *get sidetracked* — be distracted from the main task; *get tied up* — be busy and delayed; *wade through* — deal slowly with a lot of material.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To avoid doing or facing something because you are nervous, afraid or unwilling.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, sports, politics and journalism, often in the negative as praise: *She doesn't shy away from tough questions*. It takes a noun or *-ing* after *from*. Nothing goes between *shy* and *away*.
entries.pattern: (not) shy away from + noun / -ing
examples: The new principal doesn't **shy away from** difficult conversations with parents.
Many people **shy away from** talking about money, even with their own families.
After the scandal, sponsors began to **shy away from** the team.

drill.sentence: My aunt has never {{shied away from}} telling people exactly what she thinks, even at Thanksgiving dinner.
drill.hint: avoided out of nervousness (not *been afraid of*)

entries.related: *steer clear of* — deliberately avoid; *back away from* — withdraw from a plan or position; *tackle head-on* — the opposite, face it directly.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: Of an argument, claim, theory or alibi: to remain valid or convincing when examined closely.
entries.usage: Common in law, journalism, science and debate: *The claim doesn't hold up*, *hold up in court*, *hold up under scrutiny*. It is intransitive, so the claim or evidence is the subject. It is often negative or in questions like *Will it hold up?*
entries.pattern: the claim / theory / alibi holds up (under scrutiny / in court)
examples: His alibi seemed solid, but it didn't **hold up** once police checked the security footage.
The idea that cracking your knuckles causes arthritis doesn't **hold up** under scrutiny.
Several findings from that famous study have not **held up** in later research.

drill.sentence: The company's claim that its packaging is fully recyclable won't {{hold up}} if anyone looks closely.
drill.hint: stay convincing when checked (not *stand up*; not the idiom with *water*)

entries.related: *stand up* — very similar, as in *stand up in court* or *to scrutiny*; *hold water* — be logical and believable, usually negative; *fall apart* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To compare with someone or something else in quality, value or ability.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, reviews, sports and business, often in questions like *How does it stack up against the competition?* It is intransitive; the thing compared follows *against* or *to*. In British English, *doesn't stack up* on its own can also mean "doesn't make sense."
entries.pattern: how does X stack up against / to Y?
examples: How does the new iPhone **stack up against** the latest Samsung?
Honestly, my cooking doesn't **stack up** to my mom's.
On paper, the two teams **stack up** pretty evenly, so it should be a close game.

drill.sentence: We visited three colleges to see how each one {{stacked up}} against the others on cost.
drill.hint: rated in comparison (informal; not *compared* or *measured up*)

entries.related: *measure up* — be good enough, often to a standard; *compare with / to* — neutral; *hold a candle to* — usually negative, be nearly as good as.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To make use of a resource, feeling, market or source of knowledge that already exists, often to gain an advantage.
entries.usage: Common in business, marketing, politics and self-help: *tap into a market, voters' anger, your creativity, local talent*. It suggests reaching something that was already there but unused. The resource always comes after *into*.
entries.pattern: tap into + market / resource / feelings / potential
examples: The ad campaign **tapped into** parents' fears about screen time.
Good teachers **tap into** their students' curiosity instead of just lecturing.
Running early in the morning helps me **tap into** a kind of energy I don't have later in the day.

drill.sentence: The museum wants to {{tap into}} the knowledge of local veterans for its new exhibit on World War II.
drill.hint: make use of an existing source (not *draw on*)

entries.related: *draw on* — use knowledge or experience; *exploit* — use fully, often unfairly; *harness* — control and use something powerful, like energy or talent.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To accumulate a large number or amount of something, such as points, wins, debt or miles.
entries.usage: Common in sports, news and money talk: *rack up debt, points, wins, views, miles*. It can be positive (wins, views) or negative (bills, fines). The noun usually follows *up* (*rack up debt*), and a pronoun goes in the middle: *rack them up*.
entries.pattern: rack up + points / wins / debt / miles
examples: She **racked up** twenty thousand dollars in credit card debt during college.
The team has **racked up** six straight wins.
His video **racked up** two million views in a single day.

drill.sentence: Our old car had {{racked up}} over two hundred thousand miles before it finally died.
drill.hint: built up a big total of (informal; not *put on*)

entries.related: *run up* — create bills or debts, often carelessly; *clock up* — similar, more British, for miles or hours; *amass* — formal, gather a large amount over time.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To reject an idea, suggestion or proposal quickly and firmly, often without much discussion.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, families and politics: *My boss shot down my idea*. It suggests a quick and sometimes unfair rejection. A pronoun goes in the middle (*shot it down*); a noun can go before or after *down*.
entries.pattern: shoot down + idea / proposal / suggestion
examples: I suggested a road trip to Canada, but my wife **shot the idea down** in seconds.
The city council **shot down** the proposal for a new stadium.
Every time I suggest something in meetings, Greg **shoots it down** before I can finish.

drill.sentence: My parents {{shot down}} my plan to take a gap year before college.
drill.hint: rejected quickly and firmly, as if firing at it

entries.related: *turn down* — refuse an offer or request, more neutral; *veto* — officially reject, by someone with the power to do so; *reject* — the formal word.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To embrace something fully, especially something difficult, awkward or unusual, instead of resisting or hiding it.
entries.usage: A popular modern Americanism in business, media and self-help: *lean into the discomfort, the change, the joke, your image*. It suggests accepting something and turning it into a strength, but some people find it a buzzword. The thing embraced always comes after *into*.
entries.pattern: lean into + challenge / discomfort / a reputation
examples: Instead of hiding her accent, the comedian **leaned into** it and made it part of her act.
If you're nervous before a speech, try to **lean into** the feeling instead of fighting it.
The brand **leaned into** its nerdy image, and sales doubled.

drill.sentence: Everyone teased him about his terrible dancing at the office party, so he {{leaned into}} it and danced even harder.
drill.hint: accepted it fully and made it part of the fun (not *embraced* or *ran with*)

entries.related: *embrace* — more formal, accept willingly; *own it* — informal, accept something as yours without shame; *run with it* — accept an idea and develop it.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To create something, such as time, a role, a niche or a career, through determined effort.
entries.usage: Common in talk about work, business and busy lives: *carve out time, a niche, a career, a space for …*. It suggests making room where little exists, often with difficulty. The noun usually follows *out* (*carve out an hour*), and a pronoun goes in the middle: *carve it out*.
entries.pattern: carve out + time / a niche / a career / a role
examples: With three kids, I have to **carve out** time for exercise early in the morning.
The small bookstore has **carved out** a niche selling rare cookbooks.
She **carved out** a successful career as a jazz singer in a city full of rock bands.

drill.sentence: Between work and the kids, we rarely see each other, so we {{carve out}} one evening a week for date night.
drill.hint: make room for, with effort (not *set aside*)

entries.related: *set aside* — reserve time or money for a purpose; *make time for* — plainer; *find your niche* — discover the role that suits you.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To plan something carefully and in detail, step by step, before you start.
entries.usage: Common at work and in personal planning: *map out a plan, a route, a strategy, your future*. It suggests seeing the whole path in advance. The noun usually follows *out* (*map out the week*), and a pronoun goes in the middle: *map it out*.
entries.pattern: map out + plan / route / strategy / future
examples: Before the road trip, we **mapped out** every stop between Chicago and Denver.
Her parents had **mapped out** her whole future: law school, then the family firm.
The new manager spent her first week **mapping out** a strategy for the next two years.

drill.sentence: Before the renovation, the contractor {{mapped out}} every step, from demolition to the final coat of paint.
drill.hint: planned in detail, like a route (not *planned out* or *laid out*)

entries.related: *lay out* — present a plan or argument clearly; *chart a course* — plan a route or direction, more formal; *wing it* — the opposite, do it without planning.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To make something less extreme, strong or offensive, such as language, criticism, colors or behavior.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, editing, politics and fashion: *tone down the language, the rhetoric, the criticism, the makeup*. It often comes as advice or a request: *You might want to tone it down a bit*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*tone it down*); a noun can go before or after *down*.
entries.pattern: tone down + language / rhetoric / criticism; tone it down
examples: My sister asked me to **tone down** the jokes in my toast, since our grandparents would be there.
After a wave of complaints, the network **toned down** the violence in its new crime drama.
I like bold colors, but I **toned it down** for the job interview and wore navy.

drill.sentence: Your email to the landlord sounds pretty angry; maybe {{tone it down}} before you send it.
drill.hint: make it less harsh (not *soften it*)

entries.related: *play down* — make something seem less important; *soften* — make less harsh; *amp up* — the opposite, make stronger.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To treat someone badly, for example by shouting at them, because you are angry, stressed or upset about something else.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and apologies: *Don't take it out on me*, *I'm sorry I took it out on you*. The feeling (*it*, *your anger*, *your frustration*) goes between *take* and *out*, and the innocent person follows *on*. It is critical, because the person who suffers did nothing wrong.
entries.pattern: take it / your anger out on + someone
examples: I know you had a bad day at work, but please don't **take it out on** me.
Fans **took their frustration out on** the referee after the loss.
Customer service workers often get yelled at by people **taking their anger out on** the wrong person.

drill.sentence: I'm sorry I snapped at you this morning; I was stressed about the exam and {{took it out on}} you.
drill.hint: made you suffer for my bad mood (not *lashed out at*)

entries.related: *lash out at* — suddenly attack someone with angry words; *vent* — express strong feelings, not necessarily at someone; *scapegoat* — blame someone for others' faults.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To suddenly attack someone with angry words or criticism, often because you are upset or under stress.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and psychology: *lash out at critics, reporters, family*. It suggests a sudden, emotional and often unfair reaction. It is intransitive, so the target follows *at* and never comes between *lash* and *out*; it can also describe a sudden physical attack.
entries.pattern: lash out at + critics / someone (over + issue)
examples: When his manager questioned his numbers, Dan **lashed out** and accused her of never supporting him.
Teenagers who are struggling sometimes **lash out at** the people closest to them.
After a week of no sleep, I **lashed out** at my sister over a few dirty dishes.

drill.sentence: The singer {{lashed out}} at critics who called her new album boring.
drill.hint: angrily attacked in words (not *hit back* or *snapped*)

entries.related: *snap at* — speak angrily, usually briefly; *take it out on* — treat someone badly because of a different problem; *hit back at* — answer criticism with criticism.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: Of something or someone you did not like at first: to become more liked by you over time.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation about music, food, places, shows and people: *It grew on me*, *She'll grow on you*. The thing you start to like is the subject, and the person always comes after *on*. It is often used in the progressive: *It's growing on me*.
entries.pattern: something grows on someone; it's starting to grow on me
examples: I hated this song the first time I heard it, but it's really **growing on me**.
Our new neighbor seemed rude at first, but he's **grown on** us.
Living in a small town wasn't my plan, but it **grew on me** after a year or two.

drill.sentence: I didn't like coffee as a teenager, but it slowly {{grew on me}}, and now I drink three cups a day.
drill.hint: became more likable to me over time

mistake.wrong: I grew on the city after a year.
mistake.right: The city grew on me after a year.
mistake.why: The thing you start to like is the subject; the person comes after *on*.

entries.related: *warm up to* — start to like someone or something, mainly US; *an acquired taste* — something you learn to like; *wear thin* — the opposite, become annoying over time.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To decide not to take an opportunity or an offer, especially a good one.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and advice: *pass up a chance, an offer, an opportunity*, often in *too good to pass up* or with regret, as in *I can't believe I passed that up*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*pass it up*); a noun can go before or after *up*.
entries.pattern: pass up + chance / opportunity / offer; too good to pass up
examples: The flight was only eighty dollars, a deal that was too good to **pass up**.
He **passed up** a job in Paris to stay near his aging parents.
My dad never **passes up** a free sample at the grocery store.

drill.sentence: Free concert tickets? There's no way I'm {{passing that up}}.
drill.hint: letting that chance go by (not *turning down* or *missing*)

entries.related: *turn down* — refuse an offer someone makes you; *miss out on* — fail to get a good chance, often by accident; *jump at* — the opposite, accept eagerly.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To talk to someone briefly to see how they are or how something is going, or to keep them informed.
entries.usage: Very common in American workplaces and families: *I'll check in with you tomorrow*, *Just checking in*. It sounds friendly and low-pressure, so it is often used in follow-up emails. The person follows *with*, and nothing goes between *check* and *in*.
entries.pattern: check in with + someone (about + topic)
examples: I'll **check in with** you on Friday to see how the move is going.
My mom **checks in with** me every Sunday night, even though I'm thirty-five.
Good managers **check in with** new hires often during their first few weeks.

drill.sentence: Our neighbor is eighty-nine and lives alone, so a few of us take turns {{checking in with}} her every evening.
drill.hint: briefly contacting her to see how she is (phrasal verb ending in *with*)

entries.related: *check on someone* — make sure they are safe or well; *touch base* — make brief contact, mostly at work; *follow up* — contact someone again about something already discussed.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To discuss something thoroughly, often with some argument, until you reach an agreement or a solution.
entries.usage: Common at work, in politics and in families: *hash out the details, a deal, a schedule*. It suggests long and sometimes heated discussion. A pronoun goes in the middle, and *hash it out* on its own means "argue until it is settled," as in *Let them hash it out*.
entries.pattern: hash out + details / a deal / a plan; hash it out
examples: Negotiators stayed up all night to **hash out** a deal before the deadline.
My brothers and I finally **hashed out** who would take care of Dad after his surgery.
If you two disagree, go grab a coffee and **hash it out**.

drill.sentence: The landlord and the tenants met for three hours to {{hash out}} new rules for the shared yard.
drill.hint: discuss at length until they agreed (not *work out*, *sort out* or *hammer out*)

entries.related: *iron out* — solve the last small problems; *thrash out* — very similar, more common in British English; *talk through* — discuss something step by step.
